patient.chief_complaint: Two years of cognitive decline in steps, with a visual field loss that was never investigated
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Sergio Bianchi is a 76-year-old retired lorry mechanic who attends with his wife. Two years ago he noticed he could not see to the left; he stopped driving and did not seek assessment. His wife dates the beginning of his cognitive decline to the same period. He then had two further episodes: one of muddled speech lasting a day about a year ago, and one of left hand clumsiness five months ago lasting two days. After each he was permanently worse. He now cannot manage tools he used professionally, has stopped reading because he loses the left side of the page, and forgets what he has been told unless the context is given. His pulse is irregular at the bedside, which he says he has been told about before but never investigated; his sister has atrial fibrillation. He also has a right carotid bruit noted at a vascular clinic for the bypass and never imaged. He has polyvascular disease, diabetes and a 45 pack-year smoking history. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation and no dream enactment.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

medication_review.proposed: review of the current medication list for anticholinergic burden
warnings: Anticholinergic load is a reversible contributor to cognitive impairment in this population and should be quantified before any new prescription.
medication_review.summary: No prohibitive interaction identified within the current list.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Vascular dementia — multi-infarct type with two coexisting mechanisms: cardioembolism from untreated atrial fibrillation and severe symptomatic right internal carotid stenosis with a haemodynamic component

differential.key_features: The atrial fibrillation is real and anticoagulable, but it cannot explain a right internal border-zone lesion, and a severe ipsilateral stenosis with right-predominant white matter change demands its own management
The severe right stenosis explains three of the four lesions, but not the left occipital infarct in a posterior circulation territory it does not supply, and atrial fibrillation is documented
Fazekas 2 change is present and asymmetric, following the stenosis; the cortical infarct load is the substrate
Stepwise course with three dateable events, cue-responsive recall and preserved hippocampi
The visual deficit is a dense structural hemianopia from a striate infarct, not a progressive higher-order visual failure

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a collateral history from an informant who sees the patient daily: the shape of the decline (abrupt, stepwise or gradual), whether any step can be dated to a cerebrovascular event, and which instrumental activities have been lost
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Stepwise decline across three dateable events over two years, beginning with an uninvestigated hemianopia, in a patient with both an irregular pulse and an uninvestigated carotid bruit

optimal_actions.action: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MoCA 18/30 with executive and attentional impairment, cue-responsive recall and a dense left hemianopia, on a stepwise course

optimal_actions.action: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, HbA1c, lipid panel)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible causes excluded; HbA1c 8.1% and LDL 92 mg/dL above target, renal function documented for anticoagulant dosing

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms — FLAIR for white matter hyperintensity with a Fazekas grade, T1/T2 for lacunes, DWI to establish that the lesions are chronic, and SWI for microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis — together with the medial temporal atrophy grade
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Four chronic lesions of two mechanisms — right hemispheric cortical and border-zone infarcts downstream of the carotid stenosis, and a left occipital infarct from cardioembolism — with no microbleeds

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to look for atrial fibrillation as the embolic source and for the left ventricular hypertrophy of chronic hypertension
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Atrial fibrillation, never formally documented or treated — an anticoagulable embolic source

optimal_actions.action: Image the extracranial carotid arteries to establish whether a large-artery source accounts for the cortical infarcts
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Severe right internal carotid stenosis of 80-90% — a second mechanism operating alongside the atrial fibrillation, and one that must be managed on its own terms

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Left atrial enlargement with preserved systolic function and no thrombus — the substrate of the atrial fibrillation, with no additional structural source

optimal_actions.action: Treat both mechanisms: start anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation and stop the aspirin, refer for carotid revascularisation assessment for a symptomatic 80-90% stenosis with explicit discussion of the peri-procedural antithrombotic plan, avoid excessive blood-pressure lowering until the stenosis is addressed given the border-zone lesion, bring HbA1c and LDL to target for polyvascular disease, and arrange hemianopia rehabilitation with reading retraining

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

critical_actions: Establish the stepwise course and date each of the three events
Document the cardiac rhythm and recognise that an irregular pulse never investigated is an anticoagulable diagnosis
Image the carotid arteries: a bruit in a patient with ipsilateral hemispheric infarcts is not an incidental finding
Obtain MRI and assign each lesion to a mechanism by territory, because two mechanisms can coexist
Recognise the internal border-zone lesion as haemodynamic and adjust the blood-pressure strategy accordingly
Anticoagulate for atrial fibrillation and stop the antiplatelet, then plan the antithrombotic strategy around any revascularisation
Refer for revascularisation assessment of a symptomatic severe stenosis and arrange hemianopia rehabilitation
contraindicated_actions: Do not stop at the first mechanism found: atrial fibrillation and a severe ipsilateral stenosis can both be active, and treating one leaves the other untreated
Do not continue aspirin alongside a new anticoagulant outside a defined peri-procedural plan
Do not lower blood pressure aggressively while a severe stenosis with border-zone infarction remains untreated
Do not leave an uninvestigated hemianopia unexplained for two years
Do not certify fitness to drive; the hemianopia is disqualifying independently of the cognition
key_reasoning_points: Finding one mechanism does not exclude another, and here the lesion set cannot be produced by either mechanism alone: a right internal border-zone lesion is haemodynamic and a left occipital infarct is embolic
Territory assignment is the analytic tool: lesions downstream of the stenosed vessel belong to the stenosis, lesions in territories it does not supply belong to the embolic source
The two treatments interact — anticoagulation for the arrhythmia and revascularisation for the stenosis — so the antithrombotic plan must be made jointly rather than sequentially
A border-zone lesion inverts the blood-pressure strategy until the stenosis is treated
An uninvestigated hemianopia was the first stroke in this sequence, and investigating it two years ago would have identified both mechanisms before the dementia developed

red_herrings.data_point: Atrial fibrillation on the first ECG
red_herrings.intended_effect: Explains everything as cardioembolic, closes the mechanism question and leaves the carotid stenosis unimaged
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Atrial fibrillation cannot produce an internal border-zone lesion or right-predominant white matter change; a severe ipsilateral carotid stenosis is also present and needs its own management

red_herrings.data_point: A carotid bruit recorded at a vascular clinic
red_herrings.intended_effect: Dismissed as an incidental finding in a patient with known peripheral arterial disease
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A bruit ipsilateral to hemispheric infarcts in a symptomatic patient is a revascularisation question; the duplex showed 80-90% stenosis

key_educational_points: Two stroke mechanisms can coexist, and territory assignment is how they are separated
An internal border-zone lesion is haemodynamic and modifies the blood-pressure target
Anticoagulation and carotid revascularisation must be planned together, not sequentially
An uninvestigated visual field defect is often the first stroke in a sequence
